holidays.name: National Hammock Day
holidays.description: This is a day for swinging, swaying and doing nothing at all. Find two sturdy trees, string up a hammock, and treat lounging as a serious summer duty. A nap counts as participation.
holidays.origin: It's an unofficial observance with no clear founder. It fits neatly into the lazy, sun-soaked stretch of mid-July.
holidays.funFact: Hammocks were woven by Indigenous peoples of Central and South America for centuries. Sailors later adopted them because they stay steady when a ship rocks.

holidays.name: National Rat-Catcher's Day
holidays.description: This day honors the pied piper in all of us. It nods to the old trade of clearing rodents from towns and barns, and it's a good excuse to tell the legend of Hamelin.
holidays.origin: The date is tied to the legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin. Tradition says the piper led the town's children away on July 22, 1376. The holiday itself is unofficial.
holidays.funFact: The Pied Piper story is one of Germany's most famous legends. The town of Hamelin still stages summer performances of it.

holidays.name: Casual Pi Day (Pi Approximation Day)
holidays.description: This is the relaxed cousin of March 14. Written day/month, July 22 reads 22/7, a fraction that is a famous rough stand-in for pi. Math fans get a second reason to eat pie.
holidays.origin: The date comes from the fraction 22/7, which was used as an approximation of pi long before calculators. Archimedes' work on bounding pi is often credited with popularizing it.
holidays.funFact: 22/7 is about 3.142857, and real pi is about 3.141593. It's off by only about 0.04%, which is close enough for plenty of everyday jobs.
